scenes.title: Words become vectors — and vectors have no order
scenes.description: Six tokens become six points in $\mathbb{R}^4$. With no position and no mask, shuffling them only relabels the output — a theorem, and the reason positional encoding exists.
scenes.markdown:
# Words become vectors — and vectors have no order ## You are here Lit: the layer this scene builds. Dimmed: everything the lesson has yet to reach. ## The toy model card | quantity | value | |---|---| | sentence | *the cat sat on the mat* | | $n$ (tokens) | 6 | | $d_{\text{model}}$ (residual width) | 4 | | $n_{\text{heads}}$ | 2 (one shown) | | $d_k$ (per head) | 2 | $d_k \neq d_{\text{model}}$ **on purpose**. It is what makes the $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ scaling of scene 3 visibly about the *head* dimension, which is where the usual error lives. ## Tokenisation | slot | token | ID | |---|---|---| | 0 | *the* | **0** | | 1 | *cat* | 1 | | 2 | *sat* | 2 | | 3 | *on* | 3 | | 4 | *the* | **0** | | 5 | *mat* | 4 | Read it top to bottom: six entries in sentence order. Slots 0 and 4 are both *the*, so both carry ID **0** — identical tokens are identical lookups, and that repeated ID is what makes the later beat land, when the two *the*s separate only once positional encoding is added. The IDs are catalogue numbers: ID 4 is not four times ID 1, and IDs 3 and 4 (*on*, *mat*) name completely unrelated words. This list stays in the panel rather than going into the viewport, because **an index is not a location**. A token ID has no coordinate, no direction and no distance to any other token; there is nothing to plot. So step 1 draws the space and leaves it empty, with the axes unlabelled — naming them would already assert that these integers have coordinates along them. Step 2 is where the tokens enter the space, because that is where the lookup gives them vectors. ## The embedding table Row $t$ of $W_E$ is the vector for token $t$. A lookup, not a computation.
slottokenIDe1e2e3e4
0the01000
1cat10100
2sat20010
3on30001
4the01000
5mat40.50.500.5
Slots 0 and 4 are the **identical row**. Both are *the*. They separate only once positional encoding is added — that is a teaching point, not a defect. ## Reading the 3D picture $\mathbb{R}^4$ does not fit in a viewport, so one of the four coordinates has to stay off the axes. **Step 3 puts coordinate 3 on the third axis** so the choice can be watched rather than asserted: the horizontal spread does not move, five of the six tokens go flat onto the $z = 0$ sheet, and *sat* alone lifts a unit off it. **It is not that coordinate 3 carries less spread.** Measured across the six tokens: | coordinate | the six values, sorted (with $\mathrm{PE}$) | variance | range | structure | |---|---|---|---|---| | 1 | $-0.46,\ 0.14,\ 0.24,\ 0.84,\ 0.91,\ 1.00$ | $0.272$ | $1.46$ | six distinct — fast sinusoid | | 2 | $-0.99,\ -0.65,\ -0.42,\ 0.78,\ 1.00,\ 1.54$ | $0.884$ | $2.53$ | six distinct — fast sinusoid | | 3 | $0.00,\ 0.01,\ 0.03,\ 0.04,\ 0.05,\ 1.02$ | $0.1375$ | $1.02$ | one outlier over a $0.05$ band | | 4 | $1.00,\ 1.00,\ 1.00,\ 1.00,\ 1.50,\ 2.00$ | $0.1457$ | $1.00$ | three levels | Coordinates 3 and 4 have **near-identical variance** — $0.1375$ against $0.1457$, a 6% difference — and coordinate 3 has the slightly *larger* range. (Before $\mathrm{PE}$, on the raw embedding rows this step actually plots, it is $0.1389$ against $0.1458$ — the same story.) What separates them is not how much spread there is but how it is **shaped**: coordinate 3 is a binary *is this token the verb* flag, one outlier sitting above a tight band, while coordinate 4 offers three genuine levels. Coordinates 1 and 2 do the real separating, because they carry the fast positional sinusoids. So whichever of 3 or 4 takes the third axis, that axis is nearly wasted. From step 4 onward the six points plot coordinates **1, 2 and 4** on the $x$, $y$ and $z$ axes — three levels read better than one outlier — and **coordinate 3 is reported as a number**, so nothing is lost. Because *sat*'s only nonzero embedding entry is coordinate 3, it sits at the plotted origin. > **This is not dimensionality reduction.** Picking among the raw coordinate axes you were handed is a *display choice*, workable here only because this toy's coordinates happen to be interpretable one-hot-ish flags. PCA and every other real projection find directions of **high variance**, and those directions are linear combinations of coordinates — essentially never the coordinate axes themselves. "Reduce dimensions" does not mean "keep some of the dimensions you were given". ## Sinusoidal positional encoding $$\mathrm{PE}_{(p,\,2i)} = \sin\!\left(\frac{p}{10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}}}\right), \qquad \mathrm{PE}_{(p,\,2i+1)} = \cos\!\left(\frac{p}{10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}}}\right)$$ $$x_p = e_{t_p} + \mathrm{PE}_p$$ **Added, never concatenated.** The residual width stays $d_{\text{model}} = 4$ on both sides of that plus sign. A concatenation would give 8 and would change every downstream shape. $\mathrm{PE}$ is indexed by $p$, the **slot**. Shuffling the tokens moves tokens between slots; it does not move the slots. That mismatch is precisely why $\mathrm{PE}$ fails to commute with a permutation matrix, and it is the content of the proof's closing remark. RoPE — rotary position embedding, which encodes position as a *rotation* of the query and key rather than as an offset added to the embedding — is named at the end of this scene and built in scene 2. The two schemes are easy to confuse; keep them apart. ## The theorem, with its fine print $$\mathrm{Attn}(PX) = P\,\mathrm{Attn}(X)$$ holds for **a single self-attention layer with no positional encoding and no causal mask**. The regime is part of the statement, not a footnote. Two independent things break it: 1. **positional encoding** — slot-indexed, so it does not commute with $P$ (this scene); 2. **the causal mask** — row $i$'s visible key set depends on $i$, not merely on the token multiset (scene 3). ## Provenance > $W_E$, $W_Q$, $W_K$ and $W_V$ in this lesson are **hand-constructed for legibility, not learned**. They were chosen so that one head shows a clean subject–verb dependency. Real trained weights at $d_{\text{model}} = 4$ produce noise, not interpretable heads. Every figure quoted in this scene comes from the committed generation script and is asserted by `scripts/check_transformer_domain.py`; the live numbers are computed by the `transformer` domain library at `static/domains/transformer/index.js`. ## Citations - **vaswani2017** — Vaswani et al. (2017). *Attention Is All You Need.* NeurIPS. — scaled dot-product attention, sinusoidal positional encoding. - **murphy2022pml** — Murphy (2022). *Probabilistic Machine Learning: An Introduction.* MIT Press, §15.4–15.5. — definitions and shapes. - **su2021rope** — Su et al. (2021). *RoFormer: Rotary Position Embedding.* arXiv:2104.09864. — RoPE, named here and built in scene 2. ## Step notes These are the paragraphs the overlays used to carry. The overlay beside the geometry now holds only the live numbers and the one sentence you need while looking at it. ### Step 1 — an empty space, on purpose The viewport shows the sheet and nothing else. That is not a missing element: at this point the six tokens are integers, and an integer index into a table is not a position. Putting markers on screen — even "just for layout" — would quietly assert that tokens have places, spacing and order in a space they have not entered yet, and a left-to-right row of evenly spaced markers would assert the very misconception this step exists to kill: that ID 4 is somehow *more* than ID 1. The axes carry no labels for the same reason. The tokens and their IDs are listed top-to-bottom in the doc panel above, where a list belongs. ### Step 2 — lookup, not arithmetic This is where the tokens enter the space: the lookup gives each ID a vector, so each token finally has somewhere to be, and the axes get their labels in the same moment. Row $t$ of $W_E$ is the vector for token $t$: a lookup, with no arithmetic anywhere in it. Rows 0 and 4 are identical because both are *the* — identical tokens always get identical rows. The two copies of *the* land on top of each other, which is an honest consequence of the table and not an artefact of the projection. Which of the four coordinates the viewport has to give up is not asserted here — step 3 swaps coordinate 3 onto the third axis and lets you see what that axis would actually be showing you. ### Step 3 — why the third axis is dim 4, measured The third axis carries coordinate 3 for this step only. $x$ stays coordinate 1 and $y$ stays coordinate 2, so the horizontal spread is unchanged from the previous step and only the vertical moves. Five of the six tokens — *the*, *cat*, *on*, *the*, *mat* — go flat onto the sheet at $z = 0$; *sat* alone lifts a full unit. $$\bigl(\text{coord }3\bigr)_{i} = 0,\ 0,\ 1,\ 0,\ 0,\ 0$$ The tempting conclusion — that coordinate 3 was dropped for carrying less — is **false**. With $\mathrm{PE}$ on, $\operatorname{Var}(\text{coord }3) = 0.1375$ and $\operatorname{Var}(\text{coord }4) = 0.1457$: a 6% difference, and coordinate 3 has the *larger* range, $1.02$ against $1.00$. Same amount of spread, different **shape**. Coordinate 3 is one outlier at $1.02$ above a band $0.05$ wide — a binary *is this token the verb* flag. Coordinate 4 is three genuine levels, $1.0$, $1.5$, $2.0$. Either way the third axis is nearly wasted; the lesson keeps dim 4 because three levels read better than one outlier, and prints coordinate 3 as a number. And this is a **display choice among raw coordinates, not dimensionality reduction**. A real projection looks for high-variance *directions*, which are combinations of coordinates and essentially never the axes themselves. ### Step 4 — what the prediction is actually about The six points move the moment you shuffle, because the token sitting in each slot changes. That is not the question. The question is about the six **output** vectors, which stay hidden until the reveal: does the set of outputs change into something new, stay exactly the same set, or come out reordered? Grey marks everything that has not been revealed yet, and it is used for nothing else in this lesson. ### Step 5 — reading the equivariance check With the shuffle on, every live row is a frozen row at a different slot: | live slot | reads | equals frozen slot | |---|---|---| | 3 | $(0.0231,\ 0.9736)$ | 2 | | 0 | $(0.3924,\ 0.2413)$ | 5 | $$O_{\text{perm}}[k] = O_{\text{orig}}\bigl[P[k]\bigr], \qquad \max_k \bigl\lVert O_{\text{perm}}[k] - O_{\text{orig}}[P[k]] \bigr\rVert = 2.2\times10^{-16}$$ That is machine precision, not an approximation. **Regime: no positional encoding and no causal mask.** Scene 3 introduces the causal mask, which breaks equivariance for a second and completely independent reason — row $i$'s visible key set comes to depend on $i$ itself, not merely on the multiset of tokens. ### Step 6 — the width never grows $$\mathrm{PE}_{(p,\,2i)} = \sin\!\left(\frac{p}{10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}}}\right), \qquad \mathrm{PE}_{(p,\,2i+1)} = \cos\!\left(\frac{p}{10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}}}\right)$$ At full strength slot 2 (*sat*) reads $(0.9093,\ -0.4161,\ 1.02,\ 0.9998)$ — still four numbers. $d_{\text{model}} = 4$ before the plus sign and $d_{\text{model}} = 4$ after it. Positional encoding is *added* into the same four coordinates; a concatenation would read 8 and would change every downstream shape. Watch slots 0 and 4, the two copies of *the*: their embedding rows are identical, so they separate only once $\mathrm{PE}$ is switched on. ### Step 7 — two controls, one picture The amber arrows are anchored to **slots**; the cyan points are anchored to **tokens**. At PE strength 0 the shuffle merely relabels the same point set. Above 0 it genuinely moves it, because the slot did not travel with the token. That mismatch is the whole content of the proof's closing remark. There is still no causal mask here — that is scene 3's business. ### Step 8 — what is still open Sinusoidal encoding (2017) adds $\mathrm{PE}_i$ to the embedding, before the projections. RoPE (2021) instead sends $q_m \mapsto R_m q_m$ and $k_n \mapsto R_n k_n$ — a rotation applied to the query and the key, and *never* to the value. The viewport puts both operations on one real token, in the embedding space, measured from a drawn **origin**. The vector is *cat*'s embedding, $e = [0, 1, 0, 0]$, which plots to $(0, 1)$ in the two displayed coordinates, so $\lVert e \rVert = 1$ exactly. #### Both are circular Sinusoidal $\mathrm{PE}$ is a circle in position, not a straight line. With $d_{\text{model}} = 4$, $$\mathrm{PE}_p = \bigl(\sin p,\ \cos p,\ \sin\tfrac{p}{100},\ \cos\tfrac{p}{100}\bigr), \qquad \sqrt{\sin^2 p + \cos^2 p} = 1 \ \text{ for every } p$$ so the first two components ride a **unit circle** as the position sweeps. A rotation is obviously circular too. Periodicity is what the two schemes *share*: at $p = 2\pi$ and at $m\theta = 2\pi$ both pictures return to exactly where they started. #### The difference is what the circle is centred on That is the whole thing, and on screen it is one glance: **two unit circles, one centred on the origin and one centred on the tip of $e$.** **PE adds a circle-valued offset.** Its circle is centred on the tip of $e$, so the **point** $e + \mathrm{PE}_p$ orbits $e$, and its distance from the origin moves with it: $$\lVert e + \mathrm{PE}_p \rVert = \lVert (\sin p,\ 1 + \cos p) \rVert = \sqrt{2 + 2\cos p} \ \in\ [\,0,\ 2\,]$$ At $p = 0$ we have $\mathrm{PE}_0 = (0, 1)$, which lands on top of $e$ and *doubles* it to length $2.000$. At $p = \pi$ we have $\mathrm{PE}_\pi = (0, -1) = -e$, and the sum is the **zero vector** — position has cancelled the token outright. Nothing in a rotation can ever do that. **RoPE rotates.** Its circle is centred on the origin — the vector's own tail — so the **vector** turns and the length cannot move, because $R_m$ is orthogonal: $$\lVert R_m e \rVert = \lVert e \rVert = 1.000 \quad\text{for every } m$$ The overlay reads both distances live while you drag, and only one of them changes. | | sinusoidal $\mathrm{PE}$ | RoPE | |---|---|---| | shape in position | circle | circle | | what moves | the **point** $e + \mathrm{PE}_p$ | the **vector** | | circle centred on | the **tip** of $e$ | the **origin** | | distance from origin | changes, $2.000 \to 0$ | invariant, $1.000$ | | applied to | the embedding, before $W_Q, W_K, W_V$ | $q$ and $k$, after them; never $v$ | #### One thing the picture deliberately fudges Both motions are drawn on the *same* illustrative vector so the geometry can be compared side by side. Only the amber one is literal: $\mathrm{PE}$ really is added to the embedding, right there, before anything else happens. RoPE is **not** applied to the embedding. It rotates $q$ and $k$ *after* the projections $W_Q$ and $W_K$, and it is never applied to $v$ at all. Scene 2 builds it in the place it actually lives, where the query and the key exist to be rotated. The two amber controls in this scene are also different *kinds* of thing. **PE position** $p$ is a genuine position and sweeps continuously through $\mathrm{PE}_p$. The **PE strength** slider from step 6 is a $0 \to 1$ fade that brings the encoding in gradually on the token points; it is not a position, and $1$ is the honest setting. Two different schemes solving the same problem; they are easy to confuse, so keep them apart. Scene 2 builds RoPE properly: the frequencies, the relative-position property, and what the rotation does to an actual attention score. Still ahead: what $q$, $k$ and $v$ actually are; the $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ scaling; the causal mask; the second head; the block; the stack. ### Step 9 — one token, many positions The last picture in this scene puts RoPE on a token you have been looking at since step 1. *mat*'s embedding is $[0.5,\ 0.5,\ 0,\ 0.5]$ and it **never moves**. Only the position index changes, and the rotated vector changes with it — same token, different position, different representation. #### It is not one rotation RoPE does not spin the whole vector as a rigid body. It splits the $d_{\text{model}}$ coordinates into **pairs** and rotates each pair independently, at its own frequency: $$\begin{pmatrix} x_{2i} \\ x_{2i+1} \end{pmatrix} \longmapsto \begin{pmatrix} \cos p\theta_i & -\sin p\theta_i \\ \sin p\theta_i & \cos p\theta_i \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} x_{2i} \\ x_{2i+1} \end{pmatrix}$$ At $d_{\text{model}} = 4$ there are exactly two pairs, dims $(1,2)$ and $(3,4)$. Because $\theta_0 \neq \theta_1$ they never agree on where "one turn" is, and the tip traces an open curve rather than a circle. At $p = 2\pi$ the fast pair has come all the way home to $(0.5,\ 0.5)$, but the slow pair has turned only $0.35 \times 2\pi = 2.199$ rad, so dim 4 reads $-0.294$ instead of $0.5$ and **the path does not close**. That gap is the argument. What is preserved is each pair's norm, and therefore the whole vector's: $$\lVert \text{pair}_0 \rVert = 0.7071, \qquad \lVert \text{pair}_1 \rVert = 0.5, \qquad \lVert R_p e \rVert = 0.8660 \ \text{ for every } p$$ which is why RoPE can be applied at attention time without rescaling anything. #### Why *mat*, and why these frequencies A pair that is zero in the embedding cannot rotate. In this hand-built table *the* and *cat* are zero in the second pair, and *sat* and *on* are zero in the first; only *mat* has **both** pairs non-zero, so it is the only token that can show two frequencies at once. That is a property of the toy table, not a convenience. The rates on screen — $\theta_0 = 1.0$ and $\theta_1 = 0.35$ rad/position — are **illustrative**. The real schedule is $$\theta_i = 10000^{-2i/d_{\text{model}}}, \qquad \theta_0 = 1.0, \quad \theta_1 = 0.01 \ \text{ at } d_{\text{model}} = 4$$ At $0.01$ rad/position the second pair moves $0.06$ rad across the entire six-token sentence — invisible, and the trajectory would look like a single planar rotation, which is precisely the misreading this step exists to prevent. So the second frequency is exaggerated, and labelled as exaggerated. A real model has hundreds of pairs spread from $\theta \approx 1$ down to $\theta \approx 10^{-4}$: fast pairs that distinguish neighbouring tokens and slow ones that still separate positions thousands of tokens apart. Two pairs can only gesture at that. #### And it is still not the embedding The rotation is drawn on the embedding because the embedding is what is on screen. Real RoPE is applied to $q$ and $k$ **after** the projections $W_Q$ and $W_K$, never to the token embedding and never to the value $v$. The position index here is simulated. Scene 2 builds the operation where it actually lives. ### Step 10 — relative position through rotation **RoPE turns absolute rotations into relative position information through the $Q \cdot K$ dot product.** That sentence is the reason the whole scheme exists, and this step is where you can check it by hand. Two tokens: the query is *mat* at position $p$, the key is *the* at position $q$. Each is rotated to its own position by the same pair-wise rule as the previous step. The one number that matters is their dot product. #### The identity Rotations are orthogonal, so $R_x^{\mathsf T} R_y = R_{y-x}$. Each dimension pair therefore contributes $$\bigl\langle R_{p\theta_i} a_i,\ R_{q\theta_i} b_i \bigr\rangle = a_i^{\mathsf T} R_{(q-p)\theta_i}\, b_i$$ which depends on $q - p$ and on nothing else. Summing over pairs keeps that property, **even though the pairs turn at different rates** — and that is the point: RoPE can spread many frequencies across many pairs and the score stays purely relative. | $p$ | $q$ | gap | $Q \cdot K$ | |---|---|---|---| | 2 | 5 | 3 | $-0.424436$ | | 12 | 15 | 3 | $-0.424436$ | | 0 | 3 | 3 | $-0.424436$ | | 1 | 9 | 8 | $\phantom{-}0.421929$ | #### Why it *must* hold The readouts show all four terms of $$Q \cdot K = \lVert Q \rVert \, \lVert K \rVert \cos\theta$$ at once, and that is the whole explanation. A rotation is an isometry, so RoPE never changes a vector's length: $\lVert Q \rVert = 0.8660$ and $\lVert K \rVert = 1.0000$ at *every* position. And $\theta$, like the dot product, depends only on the gap — $119.35°$ at gap 3 whether the tokens sit at $(0,3)$, $(2,5)$, $(12,15)$ or $(101,104)$, and $60.84°$ at gap 8. Two of the three factors are constants of the operation and the third is fixed by the gap, so the product on the left has nothing left to vary with. Shift both positions and you are not watching a coincidence survive; you are watching an identity with no free terms. #### The general property, and the RoPE-specific instance The third slider, **global rotation**, turns $Q$ and $K$ together by a shared angle $\theta$. The dot product does not move, and this time for a reason that has nothing to do with transformers at all. For any orthogonal $R$, $$(RQ) \cdot (RK) = Q^{\mathsf T} R^{\mathsf T} R\, K = Q^{\mathsf T} K = Q \cdot K$$ because $R^{\mathsf T} R = I$. Rotate two vectors together and every angle and every inner product between them survives. That is a fact about rotations. Now the punchline. RoPE's position rotation is block-diagonal and orthogonal, so applying a shared rotation $\theta$ to both vectors is **exactly the same operation** as advancing both positions by $\theta$: $$R_\theta\,\mathrm{RoPE}(e, p) = \mathrm{RoPE}(e,\ p + \theta)$$ and the slider is implemented that way — it evaluates the same `tfRopeEmb` at $p + \theta$ and $q + \theta$. That is not a shortcut around the mathematics; it *is* the mathematics. At gap 3 the dot product reads $-0.424436244$ at $(2,5)$ and identically at $(2.5,\,5.5)$, $(3.7,\,6.7)$, $(5.3,\,8.3)$ and $(9.25,\,12.25)$. So the two controls are not two experiments. **Global rotation is the general property; shifting both positions equally is its RoPE-specific instance.** RoPE gets relative-position scores for free because it encodes position as a rotation, and rotations are exactly the operations that a dot product cannot see when both sides get the same one. The faint ghosts mark where $Q$ and $K$ sat at $\theta = 0$, so the shared sweep is visible against where it began. Move both sliders together and the vectors visibly swing somewhere else while the number holds. Move one and everything changes at once. The sliders run to 16, past the end of the six-token sentence, purely so the invariance can be tested far from where the model actually works. #### Why not *cat* and *sat* The obvious pairing does not work, and the reason is worth knowing. RoPE rotates each pair **within itself**: a token with no energy in a pair can never acquire any. This toy table is nearly one-hot, so *cat* $=[0,1,0,0]$ lives entirely in pair $(1,2)$ and *sat* $=[0,0,1,0]$ entirely in pair $(3,4)$. They start orthogonal and stay orthogonal at every pair of positions: $$\langle \mathrm{RoPE}(\textit{cat}, p),\ \mathrm{RoPE}(\textit{sat}, q) \rangle = 0 \qquad \text{for every } p,\ q$$ Every cell of the demo would read $0.000000$. **That is a limitation of the toy table, not of RoPE.** A real embedding gives every token energy in every pair, and any two tokens would show the effect. Here only *mat* $=[0.5,0.5,0,0.5]$ has both pairs non-zero, so it takes the query role; *the* $=[1,0,0,0]$ is zero in the second pair, which is why $K$ never leaves the $\text{dim }4 = 0$ plane. #### What the picture rounds off The dot product on screen is the **full four-dimensional** one, and it is exactly invariant. The drawn *angle* is not quite. Only three coordinates are drawn, and $Q$'s drawn length breathes between $0.7127$ and $0.8660$ as its second pair turns, while its true length is $0.8660$ always. So the $\theta$ printed in the overlay — the true $\mathbb{R}^4$ angle, $119.35°$ at gap 3 to a deviation of $1.4\times10^{-14}$ — is not quite the angle you can measure off the arc, which reads $119.4°$, $121.9°$ and $124.6°$ at $p = 0, 2, 12$. The arc has deliberately **not** been adjusted to agree with the number: it draws what the projection actually gives. The wobble is the projection, not the mathematics — the same lesson as coordinate 3 back in step 3. The dot product itself is not rounded off at all: because *the* is zero in the second pair, the three drawn coordinates carry the whole product, so the number beside the picture is simultaneously the true value and the drawn one. And, still: this rotates embeddings for visual intuition. Real RoPE acts on $q$ and $k$ after the projections, never on the embedding and never on $v$, and it spreads its rotations over hundreds of pairs at many frequencies. Scene 2 builds it where it lives.
scenes.prompt: Scene 1 of an open, six-scene lesson on the transformer. Scope: tokenisation, the embedding lookup, permutation equivariance, and additive sinusoidal positional encoding. Colour language, used identically in the viewport, the overlays and the proof panel: query orange #ff7043, key blue #42a5f5, value green #66bb6a, output purple #ab47bc, position amber #ffca28, token/residual cyan #26c6da. Neutral grey #9e9e9e is RESERVED for un-revealed prediction candidates and means nothing else. The weights and the embedding table are HAND-CONSTRUCTED for legibility, not learned — say so whenever they come up. The 3D points plot coordinates 1, 2 and 4 of R^4 with coordinate 3 reported numerically; state that projection whenever a plotted position looks surprising. Step 3 DEMONSTRATES that choice instead of asserting it — coordinate 3 goes on the third axis, five of six tokens go flat at z = 0 and only 'sat' lifts — so do not pre-announce it in steps 1 or 2. NEVER justify the choice by saying coordinate 3 has less variance or less spread: that is FALSE, coordinates 3 and 4 have near-identical variance (0.1375 vs 0.1457) and coordinate 3 has the larger range (1.02 vs 1.00). The reason is the SHAPE of the spread — coordinate 3 is one outlier above a 0.05-wide band, a binary verb flag, while coordinate 4 gives three levels (1.0, 1.5, 2.0); coordinates 1 and 2 carry the fast positional sinusoids and do the real separating. This caveat applies at EVERY step, not just step 3. And if asked, say plainly that choosing among raw coordinate axes is a display convenience, NOT dimensionality reduction: PCA and other real projections use high-variance directions that are combinations of coordinates, not the coordinate axes themselves. The permutation-equivariance theorem is stated ONLY for a single self-attention layer with no positional encoding and no causal mask; never quote it unqualified, and note that the causal mask (scene 3) breaks it for a second, independent reason. RoPE is named in step 8, made concrete on a token in step 9, shown to be RELATIVE in step 10, and built properly in scene 2. Step 9 rotates an EMBEDDING for intuition only — real RoPE acts on q and k after the projections and never on the embedding or v, and its two rotation rates there (1.0 and 0.35) are illustrative, not the real 1.0 and 0.01 schedule — keep the two positional schemes distinct. The lesson continues past this scene into Q/K/V, scaling and masking, multi-head attention, the full block and sampling: never present anything here as the end of the story, and do not preview what the second head attends to.

steps.title: Six tokens, six IDs
steps.description:
The sentence *the cat sat on the mat* is cut into six tokens, and each one is replaced by its catalogue number in the vocabulary. The doc panel lists them top to bottom, one token per row, which is the honest shape for this: six entries in sentence order. Slots 0 and 4 are both *the* and so carry the same ID, because identical tokens are identical lookups. The IDs are catalogue numbers, not magnitudes — ID 4 is not four times ID 1, and the IDs for *on* and *mat* sit next to each other while naming completely unrelated words.

**The viewport is empty, and that is the whole point.** A token ID is an *index into a table*, and an index is not a location: there is no coordinate to plot, no direction, no distance, nothing that would make one token nearer another. Even laying the six out in a row would be a claim — that they are ordered, evenly spaced, positioned — and that is exactly the misconception this step exists to remove. The space is drawn; the tokens are not in it, because they are not yet the kind of thing that can be in it. Nor are the axes labelled yet, for the same reason. Both the tokens and the labels arrive in the next step, when the embedding lookup turns each ID into an actual vector.

steps.title: Lookup, not arithmetic
steps.description: **This is the step where the tokens enter the space.** The embedding matrix is a **table**: row $t$ of $W_E$ is the vector for token $t$ — a lookup, no arithmetic. Each ID is replaced by the row it indexes, and only now does a token have somewhere to be. The axes get their labels in the same moment, for the same reason: there are finally coordinates for them to measure. Rows 0 and 4 are identical because both are *the*: identical tokens always get identical rows, so the two *the*s land on exactly the same point. Four dimensions do not fit in three, so one of the four coordinates has to stay off the axes. **Which one, and why, is the next step's business** — read it off the picture there rather than taking it on trust here.

steps.title: Why not dim 3?
steps.description:
The axes read *dim 1 / dim 2 / dim 4*, and that skipped **3** deserves a look rather than a promise. So the third axis is relabelled **dim 3** and the same six points are replotted against it: $x$ is still coordinate 1, $y$ is still coordinate 2, only the vertical has changed. The horizontal spread does not move at all. What changes is the third axis: five of the six tokens — *the*, *cat*, *on*, *the*, *mat* — lie flat on the sheet at $z = 0$, and *sat* alone lifts a full unit off it.

**It is not that coordinate 3 carries less spread — it does not.** Measured across the six tokens with positional encoding on, the variance of coordinate 3 is $0.1375$ and that of coordinate 4 is $0.1457$ — a 6% difference, near-identical — and coordinate 3 actually has the *larger* range, $1.02$ against $1.00$. On the raw embedding rows this step is plotting, before any $\mathrm{PE}$, it is $0.1389$ against $0.1458$ — the same story. The difference is not how much spread there is but how it is **shaped**. Coordinate 3 packs five tokens into a band $0.05$ wide and puts one outlier at $1.02$: a binary *is this token the verb* flag. Coordinate 4 gives three genuine levels, $1.0$, $1.5$ and $2.0$. Coordinates 1 and 2 are the ones doing real separating — they carry the fast positional sinusoids, and coordinate 2's variance, $0.884$, dwarfs both of the others.

So whichever of 3 or 4 takes the third axis, that axis is nearly wasted. The lesson keeps **dim 4** because three levels read better than one outlier, and **prints coordinate 3 as a number** so nothing is lost.

**One thing this is not: dimensionality reduction.** Choosing among the raw coordinate axes you were handed is a *display choice*, available here only because this toy's coordinates happen to be interpretable one-hot-ish flags. A real reduction — PCA, or any learned projection — finds directions of high variance, and those directions are combinations of coordinates, essentially never the coordinate axes themselves.

proof.title: Attention is permutation-equivariant
proof.techniqueHint: Direct computation: push a permutation matrix through each factor of the attention formula.
proof.goal: Show that $\mathrm{Attn}(PX) = P\,\mathrm{Attn}(X)$ for a single self-attention layer with NO positional encoding and NO causal mask.
proof.prompt: This proof is stated ONLY for a single self-attention layer with no positional encoding and no causal mask, and that regime is part of the theorem, not a footnote. Two independent things break it: positional encoding (PE is indexed by slot, so it does not commute with P) and the causal mask (row i's visible key set depends on i, not merely on the token multiset). This scene demonstrates the first; scene 3 retires the caveat by introducing the second. The mechanism is a side argument: P acts on the LEFT (it permutes rows, i.e. tokens) while each W acts on the RIGHT (it mixes columns, i.e. features), so they pass through each other. Softmax is row-wise, so conjugation by P survives it.

steps.label: Setup
steps.math: X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_{\text{model}}},\quad P \text{ a permutation matrix},\quad \htmlClass{hl-q}{Q = XW_Q},\quad \htmlClass{hl-k}{K = XW_K},\quad \htmlClass{hl-v}{V = XW_V}
steps.justification: Rows of $X$ are tokens; columns are features. $P$ reorders rows. There is no $\mathrm{PE}$ term and no mask $M$ — that is the regime of the claim.
steps.explanation: Three colours are bound here that the rest of the lesson keeps: **query** orange, **key** blue, **value** green. You have not seen a $q$, $k$ or $v$ vector yet — scene 2 draws them — but the colour language starts now.
steps.prompt: Establish the shapes and the regime. Stress that P is n by n and acts on rows (tokens), while each W is d_model by d_k and acts on columns (features).

steps.label: Projections commute with $P$
steps.justification: Matrix multiplication is associative, and $P$ multiplies on the LEFT while each $W$ multiplies on the RIGHT. They act on different indices, so they pass through each other.
steps.explanation: This one line is the entire mechanism. A per-token operation applied identically to every token cannot notice what order the tokens arrived in.
steps.prompt: The whole proof lives here: left action versus right action. Ask the student which index each factor touches.

steps.label: The score matrix is conjugated
steps.justification: $(PK)^{\top} = K^{\top}P^{\top}$. The scores are not new numbers: $S$ is conjugated, so rows and columns are both relabelled by the same permutation.
steps.explanation: $P$ on the left reorders which query owns each row; $P^{\top}$ on the right reorders which key owns each column. Entry $(i,j)$ of $PSP^{\top}$ is entry $(P[i], P[j])$ of $S$ — the multiset of scores is untouched.
steps.prompt: Make the conjugation concrete: entry (i,j) of P S P^T equals entry (P[i], P[j]) of S. Nothing is recomputed.

steps.label: Softmax is row-wise
steps.justification: Softmax acts independently on each row, and $P^{\top}$ only permutes entries WITHIN a row. A row's normalising sum runs over the same multiset of entries either way, so the normaliser is unchanged.
steps.explanation: This is the step the causal mask will later destroy. A mask makes row $i$'s admissible key set depend on $i$ itself, so the rows stop being interchangeable and the argument halts at exactly this line.
steps.prompt: Emphasise that softmax being row-wise is load-bearing. Foreshadow — without explaining — that the causal mask breaks this step in scene 3.

steps.justification: $P^{\top}P = I$ because $P$ is orthogonal. The trailing $P^{\top}$ is annihilated by the $P$ in front of $V$, leaving a single $P$ acting on the output.
steps.explanation: On screen: the live lattice is the frozen one with its rows permuted, to a maximum deviation of $2.2\times10^{-16}$ — machine precision. **This holds only in the stated regime: no positional encoding, no causal mask.**

A **second and independent** break arrives in scene 3 — the causal mask, which makes row $i$'s visible key set depend on $i$ rather than only on the token multiset.

Every length in the overlay is a distance from the origin, which is why the origin is drawn. THE CORRECTION THIS STEP EXISTS TO MAKE: sinusoidal PE is NOT a straight-line displacement. steps.title: Relative Position Through Rotation
steps.description: **RoPE turns absolute rotations into relative position information through the $Q \cdot K$ dot product.** Why: **rotate both vectors together and their dot product does not change** — $(R_\theta Q) \cdot (R_\theta K) = Q \cdot K$ for any shared orthogonal $R_\theta$, a fact about rotations, not about transformers. Sweep **Global rotation** (ghosts mark $\theta = 0$), then move **Q and K position** equally: the same result, because sweeping $\theta$ **is** shifting both positions by $\theta$. RoPE's position rotation is one such rotation, so the score depends only on $q-p$. Move one slider alone and everything changes at once. Doc panel for the rest.

steps.prompt: THE PAYOFF STEP of scene 1's RoPE thread, and the reason RoPE is worth the trouble. THE TAKEAWAY, which should be said in these words: RoPE turns absolute rotations into relative position information through the Q.K dot product. WHAT IS ON SCREEN: the embedding space with its origin and three labelled axes (dims 1, 2 and 4 of R^4; coordinate 3 is not plotted, as everywhere in this scene), an orange query vector Q = the token 'mat' rotated to position p, a blue key vector K = the token 'the' rotated to position q, and a white arc spanning the angle between them. The two sliders are independent. The overlay shows p, q, the gap q - p, and the dot product. THREE CONTROLS, AND THEY ARE CONCEPTUALLY TWO EXPERIMENTS THAT TURN OUT TO BE ONE. Q position and K position demonstrate RoPE and relative position. GLOBAL ROTATION theta demonstrates the underlying geometric property: apply the SAME orthogonal rotation to both vectors and angles and dot products are preserved, (R_theta Q).(R_theta K) = Q.K. That is a fact about rotations, true of any two vectors, and nothing to do with transformers. Present it that way first. THEN land the punchline: because RoPE's rotation is block-diagonal and orthogonal, applying a shared rotation theta to both vectors is EXACTLY the same operation as shifting both positions by theta — the slider is implemented as tfRopeEmb evaluated at p + theta and q + theta, and that is the mathematical content, not a shortcut. So the global rotation is the GENERAL property of which 'shift both positions equally' is the RoPE-specific instance. At gap 3 the dot product is -0.424436244 at (2,5) and equally at (2.5,5.5), (3.7,6.7), (5.3,8.3) and (9.25,12.25). Say this explicitly — it turns two knobs that look unrelated into one explanation, and it is why the step lands as a reason rather than a coincidence. Faint ghost vectors mark where Q and K sat at theta = 0 so the shared sweep is visible against its starting point; they do not move when theta does. THE IDENTITY THAT EXPLAINS EVERYTHING, and the thing to point at first: the overlay shows Q.K = |Q| |K| cos(theta) with all four terms live. A rotation is an isometry, so |Q| = 0.8660 and |K| = 1.0000 at EVERY position, and the angle theta depends only on the gap. Three of the four terms are therefore pinned the moment the gap is pinned, and the fourth cannot move. That is why the dot product is preserved — not a coincidence to be observed but an identity to be read straight off the screen. At gap 3, theta = 119.35 degrees at every placement; at gap 8 it is 60.84; at gap 2, 73.46. Ask the student which terms moved when they shifted both sliders, or swept the global rotation: none of them did. |Q| and |K| are printed in the overlay heading rather than as live figures precisely because they are constants of the operation — say so if asked why they do not tick. THE DEMONSTRATION TO WALK A STUDENT THROUGH: start at p = 2, q = 5, where Q.K = -0.424436. Now move BOTH sliders up by ten, to p = 12, q = 15. Both vectors swing to completely different absolute orientations and the dot product is STILL -0.424436, to every digit shown. p = 0, q = 3 gives it again. Then move only ONE slider: p = 1, q = 9 opens the gap to 8 and the value becomes 0.421929, with a visibly different angle. Absolute positions changed and nothing happened; the gap changed and everything did. WHY IT IS TRUE, if asked: each dimension pair contributes <R_(p.theta_i) a_i, R_(q.theta_i) b_i> = a_i^T R_((q-p).theta_i) b_i, because a rotation is orthogonal and R_x^T R_y = R_(y-x). Every term depends on q - p alone, so the sum does. It holds for all pairs at once even though they turn at different rates, which is why RoPE can use many frequencies and still be purely relative. Asserted to 1e-12 by the domain check. Do not derive it further here — scene 2 owns the derivation. WHY NOT 'cat' AND 'sat', which is the first pairing anyone asks for: RoPE rotates each dimension pair WITHIN ITSELF, so a token confined to one pair never acquires a component in the other. In this hand-built table the rows are nearly one-hot — 'cat' = [0,1,0,0] lives entirely in pair (1,2), 'sat' = [0,0,1,0] entirely in pair (3,4) — so they remain orthogonal at every pair of positions and their dot product is exactly 0.000000 everywhere, checked at (2,5), (12,15), (0,3), (1,9) and (4,4). Every cell of the demo would read zero. Say clearly that this is a limitation of the TOY EMBEDDING TABLE, not of RoPE: a real model gives every token energy in every pair, and any two tokens would work. 'mat' = [0.5, 0.5, 0, 0.5] is the only row here with both pairs non-zero, which is why it is the query; 'the' = [1,0,0,0] is zero in the second pair, so K rotates in one plane and never leaves the dim-4 = 0 plane. That is the table's doing, not a claim about keys. RANGES: the sliders run to 16, past the six-token sentence, which ends at position 5. That is deliberate and stated on screen — positions 12 and 15 exist so the invariance can be tested far from where the model actually works, not because the sentence has sixteen tokens. THE ONE PLACE THE PICTURE AND THE NUMBER DISAGREE, and you must not paper over it: the dot product shown is the FULL 4-dimensional one and it is exactly invariant. The drawn ANGLE is not quite, because only three of the four coordinates are drawn and Q's drawn length varies between 0.7127 and 0.8660 as its second pair turns, while its true length is 0.8660 always. The theta in the overlay is the TRUE angle in R^4 and is exactly invariant (119.3469 degrees at gap 3, deviation 1.4e-14 across placements). The angle you can measure off the SCREEN is not: it reads 121.9 degrees at p = 2, 124.6 at p = 12 and 119.4 at p = 0. Say which is which if a student protests that the arc looks different — the printed number is R^4, the arc is the projection, and the arc has not been faked to agree with the number. A few degrees of wobble is the projection breathing, not the invariance failing — the same 'a projection hides a dimension' point the dim-3 step made. The dot product itself is NOT approximated: because 'the' is zero in the second dimension pair, the three drawn coordinates carry the whole product, so the number beside the picture is both the true value and the drawn one. ACCURACY, NON-NEGOTIABLE AND UNCHANGED: real RoPE is applied to q and k AFTER the projections W_Q and W_K, never to the token embedding and never to v. These are embeddings standing in for a query and a key so the operation can be seen; the rotation rates 1.0 and 0.35 rad/position are illustrative, not the real 1.0 and 0.01 schedule, and a real model spreads hundreds of pairs over many frequencies. This is a 3-D projection of a high-dimensional operation — do not present it as one 3-D rotation. Scene 2 builds the real operation on the real q and k. The embedding table is HAND-CONSTRUCTED for legibility, not learned. Never suggest the lesson is finished: Q/K/V, the scaling, the mask, the second head, the block and sampling are all still ahead.

scenes.title: $Q$, $K$, $V$ — one vector, three projections
scenes.description: One token vector, three linear readings. $q$ asks, $k$ advertises, $v$ contributes — and $d_k = 2$ is not $d_{\text{model}} = 4$. Then RoPE makes query–key alignment depend only on the positional gap.
scenes.markdown:
# $Q$, $K$, $V$ — one vector, three projections ## You are here Lit: the layer this scene builds. Dimmed: what is done, and what the lesson has yet to reach. ## Shapes One token at a time, with $x_i$ a **row** vector: | product | shape | result | |---|---|---| | $x_i\,W_Q$ | $(1\times 4)(4\times 2)$ | $q_i$, $1\times 2$ | | $x_i\,W_K$ | $(1\times 4)(4\times 2)$ | $k_i$, $1\times 2$ | | $x_i\,W_V$ | $(1\times 4)(4\times 2)$ | $v_i$, $1\times 2$ | All six at once — the form an implementation actually uses: | product | shape | result | |---|---|---| | $X\,W_Q$ | $(6\times 4)(4\times 2)$ | $Q$, $6\times 2$ | | $X\,W_K$ | $(6\times 4)(4\times 2)$ | $K$, $6\times 2$ | | $X\,W_V$ | $(6\times 4)(4\times 2)$ | $V$, $6\times 2$ | | $Q\,K^{\top}$ | $(6\times 2)(2\times 6)$ | $S$, $6\times 6$ | $d_{\text{model}} = 4$ is the width of the residual stream. $d_k = 2$ is the width of **one head's** workspace. Each $W$ is $4\times 2$: not square, therefore not invertible. Two of every four input directions are discarded, and *which* two is the entire difference between $Q$, $K$ and $V$. ## The three weight matrices > **Hand-constructed for legibility, not learned.** These were chosen so that one head shows a clean subject–verb dependency. Real trained weights at $d_{\text{model}} = 4$ produce noise, not interpretable heads. Under the row-vector convention $q = xW_Q$ we have $xW = \sum_d x_d\,W[d,:]$, so **row $d$ of $W$ is the image of input basis direction $e_d$**.

Three different readings of **one** vector. At slot 2 (*sat*), $x_2 = [0.9093,\,-0.4161,\,1.0200,\,0.9998]$ gives $$q_2 = [3.0600,\; 0.9998], \qquad k_2 = [-1.2484,\; 0.9998], \qquad v_2 = [0.9093,\; -0.4161].$$ ## Scores $$s_{ij} \;=\; q_i \cdot k_j \;=\; \sum_{d=1}^{d_k} q_{id}\,k_{jd}, \qquad S = QK^{\top}.$$ Row 2 of $S$, unscaled and unmasked: | key | the (0) | **cat (1)** | sat (2) | on (3) | the (4) | mat (5) | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | $s_{2j}$ | 10.1798 | **15.1397** | −2.8206 | −7.0890 | −5.0014 | 8.6925 | These are **signed**, which is why the row lattice in the viewport uses a diverging blue–red ramp. It is the only place in the lesson where a diverging map is correct: from scene 3 onward every weight heatmap is post-softmax, hence non-negative, and uses a single-hue viridis ramp on $[0,1]$. ## Sinusoidal PE versus RoPE — the confusion site Two different answers to the same problem, and they are routinely mixed up. | | sinusoidal PE (scene 1) | RoPE (this scene) | |---|---|---| | applied to | the **embedding**, once | $Q$ and $K$, inside every head | | how | **added**: $x_p = e_{t_p} + \mathrm{PE}_p$ | **rotates** each 2D coordinate pair by $m\theta$ | | touches $V$? | indirectly, through $x$ | **never** | | score depends on | both absolute indices $m$ and $n$ | only the gap $m - n$ | | width | unchanged, $d_{\text{model}}$ | unchanged, $d_k$ | The rotation matrix is $$R_m = \begin{bmatrix}\cos m\theta & -\sin m\theta \\ \sin m\theta & \cos m\theta\end{bmatrix},$$ and the identity the proof panel establishes is $$\langle R_m q,\; R_n k\rangle = \langle R_{m-n} q,\; k\rangle.$$ **Two honesty notes.** First, $\theta = 1.0$ radian per position in the standalone demo is *illustrative*. Real RoPE uses the base-$10000$ frequency ladder of Su et al. (2021) — a different $\theta$ for each coordinate pair — which at $d_k = 2$ has exactly one pair and would be invisible. Second, the proof is written for one 2D pair; the real construction is block-diagonal over $d_k/2$ pairs, and the cancellation happens independently in each. **$V$ is never rotated.** $v_j$ carries content, not a positional question. Rotating $V$ would rotate the layer's output — a different and wrong claim, and a bug that gets shipped. In the viewport's RoPE subspace the green $v$ arrow sits still while $R_m q$ and $R_n k$ sweep. ## Step by step ### 1 · One vector, three arrows $$q_i = x_i W_Q, \qquad k_i = x_i W_K, \qquad v_i = x_i W_V$$ Row-vector convention: $x_i$ is a **row**, so each $W$ multiplies on the right. One input, three matrices, three outputs. | | value at slot 2 (*sat*) | |---|---| | $x_2$ | $[0.9093,\,-0.4161,\,1.0200,\,0.9998]$ | | $q_2$ | $[3.0600,\; 0.9998]$ | | $k_2$ | $[-1.2484,\; 0.9998]$ | | $v_2$ | $[0.9093,\; -0.4161]$ | The cyan point floats **above** the head plane: its height is layout only, not a coordinate. $\mathbb{R}^4$ is not drawn — its four numbers are printed instead. Each faint arrow leaving $x_2$ **represents the map** $W_Q$, $W_K$ or $W_V$ being applied — it is not a vector. The bold arrow from the origin is the vector that map produces: $q_2$, $k_2$ or $v_2$. Nothing here is an orthogonal projection; the maps send $x_2$ into a *different* 2-dimensional space, and the plane drawn is a picture of that space rather than a slice of $\mathbb{R}^4$. ### 2 · A projection is what it does to the basis $$W_Q = \begin{bmatrix}0&0\\0&0\\3&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\quad W_K = \begin{bmatrix}0&0\\3&0\\0&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\quad W_V = \begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&1\\0&0\\0&0\end{bmatrix}$$ Since $x$ is a row, $x W = \sum_d x_d\,W[d,:]$ — the output is a combination of the **rows**, weighted by the input coordinates. So row $d$ *is* the image of $e_d$, and each projection sends **two of four** input directions to $0$: - $W_Q$ keeps dims 3 and 4 — $e_1, e_2 \mapsto 0$ - $W_K$ keeps dims 2 and 4 — $e_1, e_3 \mapsto 0$ - $W_V$ keeps dims 1 and 2 — $e_3, e_4 \mapsto 0$ The two missing arrows under each lattice are the discarded directions; their absence is the content. Note that $W_Q$ and $W_K$ send their kept pair onto the *same little rectangle* — the same stretch in the same directions — while reading *different* input dimensions. Same destination, different source. (Both are rank 2, so each one's *image* is the whole plane; what they share is the shape of the unit square's image.) All three are hand-constructed for teaching, not learned. ### 3 · $d_k$ is not $d_{\text{model}}$ | symbol | value | what it measures | |---|---|---| | $d_{\text{model}}$ | **4** | width of the residual stream | | $d_k$ | **2** | width of one head's workspace | | $n_{\text{heads}}$ | 2 | one of them is on screen | | $n$ | 6 | tokens | $W_Q$ is $d_{\text{model}} \times d_k = 4 \times 2$. It is **not square**, so it is not invertible: half the input directions are gone. Scene 3 divides scores by $\sqrt{d_k} = \sqrt{2}$ — **not** by $\sqrt{d_{\text{model}}} = 2$. Both numbers stay on screen from here on so the two can never be confused. ### 4 · Keys advertise, queries ask At $0°$ the six live readings are the model's own raw scores for *sat*: $$[\,10.1798,\; 15.1397,\; -2.8206,\; -7.0890,\; -5.0014,\; 8.6925\,]$$ The dot product is a **length times an alignment**: a long key pointing in a lukewarm direction can outscore a short key pointing straight at you. That is part of why *cat* wins — its key is long, $4.6209$ in the first head coordinate. The rotating orange arrow is a **what-if of yours, not the model's $q$.** At $0°$ it is exactly $q_2 = [3.0600,\; 0.9998]$; any other angle is your own experiment, not a model parameter. ### 5 · A row of scores $$s_{ij} = q_i \cdot k_j = \sum_{d=1}^{d_k} q_{id}\,k_{jd}, \qquad S = QK^{\top}, \qquad (6\times 2)(2\times 6) = (6\times 6)$$ A **diverging** blue–red ramp implies a meaningful zero and a sign. Raw scores have both. Softmax outputs do not — they are non-negative and sum to one — so from scene 3 onward every weight heatmap is a single-hue (viridis) ramp on $[0,1]$, kept identical across scenes so cells stay comparable. ### 6 · RoPE: position as an angle $$R_m = \begin{bmatrix}\cos m\theta & -\sin m\theta\\ \sin m\theta & \cos m\theta\end{bmatrix}, \qquad q \mapsto R_m q,\quad k \mapsto R_n k$$ At $m = 4$: $R_4 q = [-1.3760,\; 0.3957]$. At $n = 1$: $R_1 k = [-0.8229,\; -0.5412]$. **Why a rotation and not an offset.** $R_m$ is orthogonal, so $|R_m q| = |q|$ for every $m$: the tip slides around a circle of fixed radius ($|q| = 1.4318$, $|k| = 0.9849$ for the demo vectors) and never leaves it. An *added* positional offset would push the vector off that circle and change its norm, and a vector whose length depends on where it sits in the sentence no longer means the same thing at position 2 as at position 200. Encoding position as an angle is what buys you a positional signal that costs nothing in magnitude. The angle **between** $R_m q$ and $R_n k$ is $(\arg k - \arg q) - (m-n)\theta$ — it depends on $m$ and $n$ only through their difference. For gap $3$ it is $49.4°$, and $|q||k|\cos 49.4° = 1.4318 \times 0.9849 \times 0.6511 = 0.9182$, the same number $\langle R_m q, R_n k\rangle$ reports. The amber wedge in the viewport *is* that angle: sweep $m$ and $n$ together and the wedge rotates rigidly without ever opening or closing. RoPE is applied to $Q$ and $K$ **only**. $V$ is never rotated: $v_j$ carries *content*, not a positional question, and rotating $V$ would rotate the layer's **output** — a different and wrong claim. In the standalone subspace below, $R_m q$ and $R_n k$ sweep with $m$ and $n$ while the green $v$ never moves. The lower-right figure is a **standalone illustration** — a separate 2D subspace with its own $q = [0.6,\,-1.3]$, $k = [-0.9,\,0.4]$ and $\theta = 1.0$ rad/position. Its $m$ and $n$ sliders move in steps of $0.05$ so the rotation can be *watched*, and they run to $6.3 > 2\pi$ so a **full turn** is reachable. Two honesty points about that range. The model's own positions are the integers $0$ to $5$, and the fractional values between them exist only so the motion is visible. And $5 > $ the top of the sequence is not a seventh token: at $\theta = 1.0$ the six-token sequence spans $5$ radians — about $286°$, roughly **four fifths of a turn** — so the sequence never quite closes its own circle. The slider goes further because the *rotation* is what is being explored, not the sentence. Carrying $m$ round to $2\pi$ returns $R_m q$ to exactly itself: $R_{2\pi} = I$, so the encoding is **periodic**. That is a real property of RoPE and a real limitation of a single frequency — it is why the paper uses a ladder of frequencies rather than one, so that positions far apart cannot alias onto the same angle in every coordinate pair at once. It is not the head plane above. RoPE and additive sinusoidal PE are **alternatives, never both at once**, and the domain library enforces it: switching RoPE on removes the $\mathrm{PE}$ term from $x$ altogether. This toy has no legible RoPE-only configuration to switch to — its hand-built table leans on $\mathrm{PE}$ to give *sat* a non-zero key and value, and without the added $\mathrm{PE}$ both $k_2$ and $v_2$ are exactly zero, a limit of a six-word table rather than of RoPE. So the forward pass this lesson computes stays on sinusoidal PE from end to end, and RoPE is shown here in its own subspace. ### 7 · Only the gap survives $$\langle R_m q,\; R_n k\rangle \;=\; \langle R_{m-n} q,\; k\rangle$$ Verified anchors: $(m,n) = (4,1) \Rightarrow 0.918150$, $(3,0) \Rightarrow 0.918150$, $(9,6) \Rightarrow 0.918150$. Same gap, same number, to machine precision. The two absolute indices go in; only their difference comes out. That is the property additive positional encoding does **not** have, and it is what makes extending a model's context length *possible* — but not free. Plain RoPE **degrades** past the length it was trained on; the methods that actually work are rescalings of the frequency ladder — Position Interpolation (Chen et al., 2023), NTK-aware scaling, YaRN (Peng et al., 2023) — and the same failure is part of what motivated ALiBi (Press et al., 2022). The identity above is what those methods have to work with; it is not a guarantee on its own. We now have scores. **Scene 3 turns scores into a distribution.** ## Provenance > Every figure quoted in this scene comes from the committed generation script and is asserted by `scripts/check_transformer_domain.py`; the live numbers are computed by the `transformer` domain library at `static/domains/transformer/index.js`. The weights are designed for teaching, not learned. ## Citations - **vaswani2017** — Vaswani et al. (2017). *Attention Is All You Need.* NeurIPS. — the $Q/K/V$ projections, $d_k$ per head, scaled dot-product attention. - **su2021rope** — Su et al. (2021). *RoFormer: Rotary Position Embedding.* arXiv:2104.09864. — RoPE, the relative-position identity, and the base-$10000$ frequency ladder. - **murphy2022pml** — Murphy (2022). *Probabilistic Machine Learning: An Introduction.* MIT Press, §15.4–15.5. — shapes and definitions.
scenes.prompt: Scene 2 of an open, six-scene lesson on the transformer. Scope: the Q/K/V projections, the head dimension d_k, the raw score row, and RoPE. Colour language, identical in the viewport, the overlays and the proof panel: query orange #ff7043, key blue #42a5f5, value green #66bb6a, output purple #ab47bc, position amber #ffca28, token/residual cyan #26c6da. Neutral grey #9e9e9e is RESERVED for un-revealed prediction candidates and appears nowhere in this scene - there is deliberately NO prediction step here; scene 2 is the rest point between scene 1's theorem and scene 3's density, so slow down rather than compress, and answer anything asked. Non-negotiables. (1) Q, K and V are never three inputs: they are three linear readings of ONE vector, and the difference between them is which input dimensions each keeps - W_Q reads dims 3 and 4, W_K dims 2 and 4, W_V dims 1 and 2. (2) d_k = 2 and d_model = 4 are different numbers and both stay on screen; the scaling constant of scene 3 is sqrt(d_k), never sqrt(d_model). (3) RoPE is applied to Q and K ONLY, never to V and never to the embedding; v_2 is bit-identical with the toggle on and off, and rotating V is a real shipped bug. (4) theta = 1.0 rad/position in the standalone RoPE demo is illustrative, not the paper's base-10000 ladder, which at d_k = 2 has a single coordinate pair and is invisible; say so when RoPE frequencies come up. (5) The rotating query arrow in the head plane is the STUDENT's what-if probe, not a model parameter - at 0 degrees it is exactly the model's q_2. (6) W_Q, W_K, W_V and the embedding table are hand-constructed for legibility, not learned; say so whenever they come up. (7) The point above the head plane is x_2 in R^4; its height is layout only and R^4 is not drawn - its four coordinates are printed instead. The three faint arrows leaving x_2 REPRESENT the learned maps W_Q, W_K, W_V; they are not vectors and not the results of those maps. The bold in-plane arrows from the origin are the results: q_2, k_2, v_2. This is NOT an orthogonal projection of x_2 onto a plane inside R^4 - the maps send x_2 into a DIFFERENT 2-dimensional space, and the drawn plane is a picture of that space, not a subspace of R^4. Never describe q_2, k_2 or v_2 as shadows or projections of x_2. Softmax, scaling and the causal mask all belong to scene 3: name them as coming, never compute them here. The lesson continues past this scene into scaled masked attention, multi-head, the block and sampling: never present anything here as the end, and do not preview what the second head attends to.

steps.title: One vector, three arrows
steps.description: $q$, $k$ and $v$ are **not three inputs**. They are three *learned linear maps* applied to the same vector $x_2$: $q$ asks *what am I looking for*, $k$ advertises *what I can offer*, $v$ carries *what I would contribute*. The three faint arrows leaving $x_2$ are those maps — $W_Q$, $W_K$, $W_V$ — **not** their results. Each map lands in the head space, and the vector it produces there ($q_2$, $k_2$, $v_2$) is drawn boldly from that space's origin. Nothing here is an orthogonal projection: $x_2$ lives in $\mathbb{R}^4$ and these maps send it into a **different**, 2-dimensional space. The plane is a *picture of that space*, not a slice of $\mathbb{R}^4$ — and the height of $x_2$ above it is layout only.

steps.title: A projection is what it does to the basis
steps.description: With the row-vector convention $q = x W_Q$, the image of basis direction $e_d$ is the $d$-th **row** of $W_Q$. The projection literally throws information away. $W_K$ throws away a *different* pair, and $W_V$ a different pair again. That is the whole difference between the three: not three inputs, three different things **kept**.

info.title: Rows are basis images
info.content: $xW = \sum_d x_d\,W[d,:]$, so row $d$ **is** the image of $e_d$. $W_Q$ reads dims 3, 4 · $W_K$ dims 2, 4 · $W_V$ dims 1, 2 — each sends the other two directions to $0$.

info.title: Rotation keeps length
info.content: Each tip rides **its own circle** — a rotation cannot change a length, where an added offset would. The amber wedge is the angle between the arrows, and the gap $m-n$ alone sets it. $V$ is never rotated.

steps.prompt: Two objects on screen and they must not be conflated. (1) The standalone RoPE subspace bottom-right: its own demo vectors q = [0.6,-1.3], k = [-0.9,0.4], theta = 1.0 rad/position, driven by m and n. (2) The main head plane above, which is NOT rotated and does not respond to this step: the forward pass this lesson computes uses additive sinusoidal PE throughout. THE GEOMETRY IS THE POINT HERE. Each tip rides a circle of fixed radius (|q| = 1.4318, |k| = 0.9849): a rotation preserves length, which is exactly why position is encoded as an angle rather than as an added offset - an offset would move the vector off its circle and change its norm, and with it the vector's own self-similarity. The encoding is also PERIODIC: carry m round to 2*pi and R_m q returns to exactly itself, which is what the full-turn range exists to show. RANGE HONESTY, state it plainly if asked: the model's own positions are the integers 0 to 5, so at theta = 1.0 the six-token sequence spans 5 radians - about 286 degrees, roughly four fifths of a turn, not quite a full circle. The sliders run to 6.3 so the student can close the circle and see the periodicity; values past 5 are exploring the ROTATION and do not claim a seventh token, and the fractional values between integers exist only so the motion can be watched. The amber wedge is the angle between the two arrows; its opening is a function of m - n alone, which is the next step's theorem made visible, and it holds under a shared shift of any size including one that wraps past 2*pi. RoPE AND ADDITIVE PE ARE ALTERNATIVES, NEVER BOTH: the domain library forces the PE term out of x whenever RoPE is switched on, because no model applies a sinusoidal offset and then rotates the result. That is also why the head plane above is not wired to a RoPE switch. Say plainly, if asked, that this toy has no legible RoPE-only configuration: its hand-built embedding table leans on PE to give 'sat' a non-zero key and value, and without the PE term k_2 and v_2 are exactly zero - a limit of the six-word table, not of RoPE. Rotating V is a real implementation bug people ship. Be honest that theta = 1.0 is illustrative: the paper uses a base-10000 frequency ladder with one frequency per coordinate pair, which at d_k = 2 is a single pair and would be invisible. proof.title: RoPE encodes relative position
proof.techniqueHint: Direct computation resting on one fact: rotation matrices are orthogonal and compose by adding angles.
proof.goal: Show that $\langle R_m q,\; R_n k \rangle = \langle R_{m-n} q,\; k \rangle$ — the inner product depends on the positions $m$ and $n$ only through their difference.
proof.prompt: Proof 3 of the lesson. It is deliberately scaffolded EXPLORATION FIRST: by the time a student opens this panel they have already dragged m and n in the last step and watched the score refuse to move. The panel explains a fact they have already observed. Keep the colour language: q orange, k blue, the position indices amber - the theorem happens visually when the two amber indices m and n collapse into a single amber n-m. Two honesty points. First, theta = 1.0 rad/position here is illustrative; real RoPE uses a base-10000 frequency ladder with one frequency per coordinate pair, which at d_k = 2 has exactly one pair. Second, the argument is stated in one 2D pair; real RoPE block-diagonalises into d_k/2 such pairs and the same cancellation happens independently in each. scenes.title: Scaled dot-product attention — a hand-built subject→verb head
scenes.description: One query, five stages, real numbers: raw score $\to$ scale by $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ $\to$ mask $\to$ softmax $\to$ weighted sum. Then the same computation for all six queries at once, as $QK^{\top}$.
scenes.markdown: # Scaled dot-product attention — a hand-built subject→verb head Every number in this scene comes from one head whose $W_Q, W_K, W_V$ were chosen by hand so that the verb attends to its subject. It is a toy built to be legible, not a trained model; the mechanism is real, the pattern is staged. ## You are here Lit: the layer this scene builds — **one head of it**. Dimmed: everything the lesson has yet to reach. ## The five stages For one query index $i$: 1. **raw score** — $s_{ij} = q_i \cdot k_j$, a signed number, one per key. 2. **scale** — divide by $\sqrt{d_k} = \sqrt{2}$. Not $\sqrt{d_{\text{model}}} = 2$. 3. **mask** — add $-\infty$ (in code, $-10^{9}$) to every entry with $j > i$. 4. **softmax** — exponentiate and normalise. The row becomes a distribution. 5. **weighted sum** — $o_i = \sum_j \alpha_{ij} v_j$. Stages 3 and 4 are in that order and the order is not a convention. See the mask-order table below. $$\mathrm{Attn}(Q,K,V) = \mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_k}} + M\right)V$$ ## Step by step The on-screen panels are pointers. The reasoning lives here. **1 · Half A — one query at a time.** We walk one query through all five stages with real numbers before doing all six at once, because a $6\times6$ lattice hides what a $1\times6$ row shows. Nothing in this step is new: scene 2 already produced the row $s_{2j}$. What is new is that it is now stage one of a pipeline. Each cell also stands off the plane by its value (one cell of height per ten points; a negative score sinks), so the same number is read twice, as colour and as relief. The ramp is **diverging** because raw scores genuinely carry a sign — the last place in the lesson where that is true. From the softmax onward every weight lattice is a single-hue viridis ramp on $[0,1]$, identical across scenes so cells stay comparable. **2 · Predict.** The row on screen is row **3** (*on*), not row 2, and the choice is deliberate: row 2 is saturated and would barely move, hiding the very effect being taught. The causal mask is still off here — all six keys are visible, and stays that way until step 5, so nothing on screen depends on a rule the lesson has not introduced. Grey means *un-revealed*. Commit to sharper, flatter, or a new winner before dragging. **3 · Reveal.** Flatter, same winner. Dividing every entry by one positive constant is monotone, so the ordering cannot change; the top weight of the unmasked row falls $0.4167 \to 0.3365$. The misconception control divides by $\sqrt{1}$, $\sqrt{d_k}$ or $\sqrt{d_{\text{model}}}$ — on the flagship entry $s_{21}$ that is $15.1397$, $10.7054$ and $7.5699$. $d_k$ is the *per-head* width; $d_{\text{model}}$ never divides anything. **4 · The seam.** See *Why $\sqrt{d_k}$* below. The pink object is not the toy, and it is drawn in a colour outside the $q/k/v/o$ palette for exactly that reason. **5 · Predict.** One question: what the mask removes, and whether the survivors keep their values. It is one question on purpose — the second one, why a mask beats feeding the model six truncated prefixes, cannot be reasoned out from anything on screen, so it is *told* in the reveal rather than asked. This prediction sits two steps after the previous one on purpose — back-to-back predictions train casual guessing. **6 · Reveal.** See *Mask before softmax* below. Structurally, the mask is what makes a single forward pass a legal simultaneous evaluation of every factor $p(x_t \mid x_{ query \ keythecatsatonthematrow sum 0 the1.0000·····1.0000 1 cat0.49140.5086····1.0000 2 sat0.02910.97090.0000···1.0000 3 on0.17600.19510.13430.4946··1.0000 4 the0.21180.24300.14770.25860.1390·1.0000 5 mat0.15310.18180.09760.23450.09040.24251.0000 The cells are rounded to 4 dp *independently*, so adding the printed digits in rows 4 and 5 gives 1.0001 and 0.9999. The **row sums above are the sums of the unrounded values**, and the viewport prints `tfRowSum(i)` at six decimals so you can check that claim rather than take it. Row 2 is the flagship: the verb *sat* puts $0.970889$ of its mass on its subject *cat*, and $0.000003$ on itself. Its output is $o_2 = (0.8461,\ 1.5246)$. ## Mask before softmax, or the row is not a distribution | | $\alpha_{2j}$ | $\sum_j \alpha_{2j}$ | |---|---|---| | **mask on the scores, then softmax** (correct) | $[0.029108,\ 0.970889,\ 0.000003,\ 0,\ 0,\ 0]$ | $1.000000$ | | **softmax over all six, then zero the future** (wrong) | $[0.0288,\ 0.9611,\ 0.0000027,\ 0,\ 0,\ 0]$ | $0.989933$ | The wrong order silently deletes $1.0067\%$ of the row's probability mass. Nothing throws; the picture looks almost identical; every downstream number is quietly off. Toggle **mask AFTER softmax (wrong)** in the viewport and read the two sums side by side at six decimals. Why $-\infty$ on the scores is legitimate at all is proof 5 in the panel: softmax is invariant to adding a constant to every entry, so it is an operation that lives naturally on the *scores*. In code the $-\infty$ is $-10^{9}$, a large finite number, so no `NaN` ever reaches the renderer. ## Read across, never down $A$ is **row-stochastic**: each row is a distribution over keys, and different rows were normalised by different denominators. Comparing two cells in the same *column* — "the model attends more to *cat* here than there" — compares numbers that were never on a common scale. Every honest reading of an attention heat map is a reading *along a row*. ## Why $\sqrt{d_k}$, and what our toy cannot show you Dragging the scaling slider shows a **symptom**: an unscaled row is sharper. It cannot show you why the constant is $\sqrt{d_k}$, because $W_Q$ and $W_K$ here were built by hand and the resulting $q$ and $k$ are neither random nor independent. So the scene puts a **second, generic object** on screen: pairs of vectors whose $2d_k$ components are fully mutually independent, zero-mean and unit-variance. For those, $\mathrm{Var}(q\cdot k) = d_k$ exactly, which is proof 2. | $n$ | empirical $\mathrm{Var}(q\cdot k)$, 2,000,000 draws | theory | |---|---|---| | 2 | $2.0003$ (mean $-0.00008$) | $2$ | | 64 | $64.10$ | $64$ | The figure the viewport prints is your own much smaller run — 4,000 draws — and it wobbles. The table above is the anchor. This is an **initialisation-time** argument, and it is exactly what it claims to be. After training, $q$ and $k$ are neither unit-variance nor independent, and the logit scale drifts — which is why QK-normalisation (Dehghani et al., 2023; used in OLMo 2 and Gemma 3) applies a norm to $q$ and $k$ before the dot product and lets a learned scale take over. It does not weaken the constant: at initialisation $\sqrt{d_k}$ is the unique divisor that restores unit variance. The "it prevents vanishing gradients" story is a **corollary**, not the reason. Large-variance logits saturate softmax, and a saturated softmax has a small Jacobian; but that follows *from* the variance fact, and quoting only the consequence is how this became folklore. ## Softmax and temperature This scene uses softmax at temperature $1$ and does not vary it. Temperature, top-$k$ and nucleus sampling belong to the decoding step, not to attention, and the lesson reaches them later. ## Attention is not explanation A large $\alpha_{ij}$ is a fact about the mixing weights. It is **not** evidence that the model's output depends on token $j$. Jain and Wallace (2019) show that alternative attention distributions can leave predictions unchanged and that adversarial attention patterns can be constructed with the same outputs; Wiegreffe and Pinter (2019) rebut this in part, arguing the claim depends on what one demands of an explanation. This lesson teaches the **mechanism** and makes no interpretability claim. ## Provenance > The weights $W_Q$, $W_K$, $W_V$ and the embedding table are **hand-constructed for legibility, not > learned**. Real trained weights at $d_{\text{model}} = 4$ produce noise, not a clean subject-verb > head. Every figure quoted here is asserted by `scripts/check_transformer_domain.py`; the live > numbers come from `static/domains/transformer/index.js`. ## Citations - **vaswani2017** — Vaswani et al. (2017). *Attention Is All You Need.* NeurIPS. — scaled dot-product attention, the $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ constant and its variance justification, the causal mask. - **murphy2022pml** — Murphy (2022). *Probabilistic Machine Learning: An Introduction.* MIT Press, §15.4–15.5. — shapes, softmax, row-stochastic attention. - **murphy2023pmlat** — Murphy (2023). *Probabilistic Machine Learning: Advanced Topics.* MIT Press. — the masked decoder-only formulation. - **jain2019attention** — Jain & Wallace (2019). *Attention is not Explanation.* NAACL. — and Wiegreffe & Pinter (2019), *Attention is not not Explanation*, EMNLP. - **poloclub-transformerexplainer** — Cho et al. Transformer Explainer, Georgia Tech. — an interactive reference for the same pipeline at scale. - **3b1b-attention** — 3Blue1Brown, *Attention in transformers, visually explained.* — the query/key geometric intuition.

Scene 3 of an OPEN six-scene lesson on the transformer. Scope: scaled dot-product attention for ONE head. Colour language, identical in viewport, overlays and proof panel: query orange #ff7043, key blue #42a5f5, value green #66bb6a, output purple #ab47bc, position amber #ffca28, token/residual cyan #26c6da, causal mask slate #455a64. Red #e53935 is RESERVED for a deliberate error (the 0.989933 broken row sum, the wrong divisor). Neutral grey #9e9e9e is RESERVED for un-revealed prediction candidates and appears only in steps 2 and 5. Pink #f06292 belongs to the GENERIC i.i.d. object of step 4 and to nothing else - its being outside the q/k/v/o palette is the point.

STRUCTURE, never reorder: half A (steps 1-9) is one query at full numeric detail; step 9 is the 'a weighting is not an explanation' rest beat; half B (steps 10-11) vectorises to QK^T. Half B does not begin before half A has asserted the row sum on screen (step 7).

Non-negotiables.
(1) The scaling divisor is sqrt(d_k) = sqrt(2), NOT sqrt(d_model) = 2. Both numbers stay on screen. tfScoreDiv(2,1,2) = 10.7054 and tfScoreDiv(2,1,4) = 7.5699 - the misconception has a price and it is visible.
(2) NEVER give 'it prevents vanishing gradients' as the REASON for sqrt(d_k). The reason is that Var(q.k) = d_k for fully mutually independent zero-mean unit-variance components; the gradient story is a corollary of that.
(3) NEVER claim the toy Q/K demonstrate proof 2's hypothesis. If a student asks 'so does our matrix prove that?', the honest answer is NO - the hand-built W_Q, W_K give q and k that are neither random nor independent. The scaling slider shows the SYMPTOM on the toy; the generic i.i.d. object of step 4 shows WHY the constant is what it is. That seam is a stated honesty commitment, not a stylistic choice, and the bottom-right overlay states it permanently.
(4) The mask is applied to the SCORES, before softmax. Applying it after gives 0.989933 instead of 1.000000 for row 2 - the single most common visualization error in the subject. Never present the two orders as alternative conventions.
(5) Steps 2 and 5 are PREDICT steps. You are FORBIDDEN from answering the prediction, hinting at the answer, or narrowing the options, no matter how the question is phrased. Ask the student to commit out loud first, then tell them to advance the step.
(6) The attention matrix is row-stochastic. Reading down a column is meaningless; say so.
(7) The weights are HAND-CONSTRUCTED for teaching, not learned. Say so whenever asked about them or about the 97.09% figure; the bottom-left overlay carries this permanently.
(8) A large attention weight is not an explanation of the model's output (Jain & Wallace 2019; Wiegreffe & Pinter 2019 in partial rebuttal). Never let 'sat attends to cat' become 'sat attends to cat because cat is the subject'.
(9) There is exactly ONE head on screen and the scene says so. Scene 4 owns the prediction 'which token will head 2 attend to?' - do NOT answer it, preview head 2's pattern, or hint at it. Do NOT summarise the lesson or imply the forward pass is complete: scenes 4, 5 and 6 are still ahead.
(10) -1e9 stands in for -infinity so no NaN reaches the renderer. Do not claim the code literally uses -Infinity.

This scene is at the cognitive ceiling. Answer narrowly, do not volunteer downstream material, and prefer pointing at a number already on screen over introducing a new one. proof.title: Why the constant is $\sqrt{d_k}$
proof.techniqueHint: Direct computation: the variance of a sum of independent products. Every step is elementary; the content is entirely in which independence hypothesis is needed and where.
proof.goal: If $q, k \in \mathbb{R}^{d_k}$ have **fully mutually independent** components — all $2d_k$ of them, across both vectors, not merely identically distributed within each — each with mean $0$ and variance $1$, then $\mathbb{E}[q\cdot k] = 0$ and $\mathrm{Var}(q\cdot k) = d_k$; so dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$ restores unit variance.
proof.prompt: Proof 2 of the lesson, bound to the GENERIC i.i.d. beat and to nothing else. The single most important thing about it: it is NOT a statement about this lesson's toy Q and K. The toy's W_Q and W_K were hand-built, so its q and k are neither random nor independent, and the scaling slider two steps earlier showed only the SYMPTOM. If a student asks 'so our matrix proves this?', the answer is no - and the reason a second object exists on screen is exactly that. The hypothesis is FULL MUTUAL INDEPENDENCE across all 2 d_k components; the cross-covariance step is where it is spent, and a weaker 'identically distributed within each vector' hypothesis makes the theorem false. The gradient story - large-variance logits saturate softmax, and a saturated softmax has a small Jacobian - is a COROLLARY, never the justification; stating only the consequence is how this became folklore. Finally, d_k is the PER-HEAD width, 2 here, and d_model = 4 never enters the constant.
