If a student offers 'it prevents vanishing gradients' as THE reason, correct it gently and show why: the gradient story is compatible with any large-enough divisor, whereas sqrt(d_k) is the unique one that gives unit variance.

steps.label: Our toy does not satisfy this
steps.justification: $W_Q$ and $W_K$ in this lesson were chosen by hand so that one head would show a clean subject-verb dependency. The resulting $q_i$ and $k_j$ are deterministic, and $q$ and $k$ both derive from the same $x_i$ — so they are neither random nor independent.
steps.explanation: This is the seam, and it is stated here as well as on screen. The scaling slider showed you a **symptom** on the toy: an unscaled row is sharper. This theorem fixes the **constant**, and to do that it needs vectors the toy does not have. Two objects, two jobs — and pretending one does both jobs would be this lesson's most serious honesty failure.
steps.prompt: Restate the seam plainly whenever asked. The toy shows the symptom; the generic i.i.d. object justifies the constant. If a student asks whether our 6x6 demonstrates Var(q.k) = d_k, the answer is a clean no, with the reason.

steps.label: This is an argument about initialisation
steps.math: \mathrm{Var}(q\cdot k) = d_k \quad\text{holds at init}\qquad\text{but}\qquad q, k \ \text{after training are neither unit-variance nor independent}
steps.justification: The hypothesis is a statement about the distribution the parameters are drawn from, not about the parameters a trained model ends up with. Nothing in the calculation survives the loss of independence or of unit variance.
steps.explanation: The constant is still right, and right for this reason: at initialisation $\sqrt{d_k}$ is the unique divisor that returns the logits to unit variance. What the argument does **not** license is the belief that the logit scale stays put once training moves the weights. It does not, which is why **QK-normalisation** (Dehghani et al., 2023, *ViT-22B*; shipped in OLMo 2 and Gemma 3) normalises $q$ and $k$ before the dot product and hands the scale to a learned parameter.
steps.prompt: Do not let this be heard as a retraction. The variance argument is correct at initialisation, which is all it claims; the remark only bounds its scope. If a student asks why anyone needs QK-norm when sqrt(d_k) exists, the answer is that sqrt(d_k) fixes the scale for the distribution the weights START from, and training moves them.

proof.title: Softmax is shift-invariant
proof.techniqueHint: Direct: a common factor cancels. Two lines, shown in full — hiding them behind a progressive reveal would be theatre.
proof.goal: $\mathrm{softmax}(z + c\mathbf{1}) = \mathrm{softmax}(z)$ for any scalar $c$ — adding the same number to every score changes nothing.
proof.prompt: Proof 5, the shortest in the lesson, and it is on screen because it licenses two things the student has just seen. First, the standard implementation subtracts max_j z_j before exponentiating, purely to avoid overflow, and this identity is why that is free. Second, an additive -infinity on masked entries is a coherent operation precisely because softmax lives naturally on additive changes to the scores: e^{-inf} = 0 removes the term and the survivors renormalise into a genuine distribution. In this lesson's code -infinity is -1e9, a large finite number, so no NaN reaches the renderer - say so if asked; do not claim the code uses -Infinity literally. This is a licence for the mask's PLACEMENT, not for its order: masking after softmax is still wrong, and gives 0.989933.

steps.label: Factor the shift out

pos.label: the shift constant $e^{c}$ — a neutral marker, not the position colour. It appears in numerator and denominator and cancels.

steps.justification: $e^{z_j + c} = e^{c}e^{z_j}$, and the constant $e^{c}$ factors out of the sum in the denominator. It is strictly positive, so the cancellation is always legal.
steps.explanation: That is the whole proof. Softmax cares about *differences* between scores and nothing else — which is another way of saying the scores have no absolute zero.
steps.prompt: Two lines, no scaffolding. The cancellation is exact and needs only that e^c is positive. Stress the reading: softmax sees only differences between scores.

steps.label: Two consequences

mask.label: the additive mask — the slate (#455a64) cells of the lattice in the viewport

steps.justification: Subtracting the row maximum leaves the output unchanged and keeps every exponent at most $0$, which is the standard numerically stable implementation. And an additive $-\infty$ is just another additive change to the scores: $e^{-\infty} = 0$ deletes the term, and the surviving entries still normalise to $1$.
steps.explanation: This is the licence for **where** the mask goes — on the scores, as an additive term — not for what order it goes in. Masking after softmax deletes mass instead of redistributing it, and gives $0.989933$ for row 2 where a distribution requires $1.000000$. In the code the $-\infty$ is $-10^{9}$, a large finite number, so the renderer never sees a `NaN`.
steps.prompt: Connect the symbols to the viewport: the hl-mask spans are the dark cells of the causal lattice. Two consequences, and keep them distinct - max subtraction is a numerics trick, the additive -infinity is the mask itself. Neither licenses masking AFTER softmax.

proof.title: The output lies in the convex hull of the values
proof.techniqueHint: Definitional: once softmax has given non-negative weights that sum to one, 'convex combination' is exactly what the output already is.
proof.goal: $o_i = \sum_{j \le i} \alpha_{ij} v_j \in \mathrm{conv}\big(\{v_j : j \le i\}\big)$ — a single attention head cannot produce a direction that no visible value carries.
proof.prompt: Proof 4, deliberately scaffolded exploration-first: by the time a student opens this panel they have already dragged the query and watched the output point refuse to leave the shape. The panel explains something they have already seen. The argument is definitional and that is not a weakness - the content is in what it RULES OUT. Two precisions. First, with the causal mask on the relevant hull is conv{v_j : j <= i}, not the hull of all six values; the viewport hides the forbidden value points, so at i = 2 the reachable region is the triangle on the three that remain. Second, the viewport draws the value points at 2x scale and offset, for legibility; the coordinates in the panel are the true ones. The conclusion is a forward hook - expressive power lives in W_V, W_O, the feed-forward block and depth, all of which later scenes handle. Name them and stop.

steps.label: What softmax guarantees

v.label: the weights — non-negative and summing to one, the same green as the hull

steps.justification: Every $\alpha_{ij}$ is $e^{\cdot}$ over a sum of positive terms, so it is positive; the denominator is exactly the sum of the numerators, so the row sums to $1$. The masked entries contribute $e^{-\infty} = 0$ and drop out of the sum entirely.
steps.explanation:
These two properties are not extra assumptions — they are what softmax *is*. The viewport prints the row sum at six decimals in the previous step precisely so this line is checkable rather than asserted.

Green here is the *weights*, on the green *values* they weight — the colour is doing double duty on purpose, because the whole claim is that the two live in the same convex set.
steps.prompt: Point back at the asserted row sum from the softmax step: this given is already on screen at six decimals. Non-negativity and summing to one are definitional properties of softmax, not additional hypotheses.

steps.label: That is the definition of a convex combination

v.label: the coefficients — and the value points and hull they weight

o.label: the output point — the purple dot in the viewport

steps.justification: The convex hull of a finite point set is *defined* as the set of all non-negative combinations of those points whose coefficients sum to one. The left-hand side is literally an element of that set.
steps.explanation: There is no inequality to prove and nothing to estimate. The step is worth making anyway, because naming the object tells you what it forbids — and forbidding is where the content is.
steps.prompt: Say plainly that this is definitional, and that the definitional character is not a weakness: it means the constraint holds for every input, every weight matrix and every training run, not just for this toy.

steps.label: What attention cannot do

o.label: the output — it has nowhere else to go

v.label: no choice of weights escapes the hull

steps.justification: No setting of the scores, the temperature, the scaling constant or the mask can move $o_i$ outside the hull, because all of those act only through the $\alpha_{ij}$, and every admissible $\alpha$ gives a point inside.
steps.explanation:
So a single head **mixes**; it does not create. At $i = 2$ the output $(0.8461,\ 1.5246)$ sits almost on top of $v_1 = (0.8415,\ 1.5403)$, because $0.970889$ of the weight is there.

Expressive power has to come from somewhere else: from $W_V$, which chooses what the values *are*; from $W_O$; from the feed-forward block; and from depth. The lesson reaches all four — they are ahead, not here.
steps.prompt: The misconception killed: 'attention can produce any output'. It cannot - mixing is bounded by what is being mixed. This is a forward hook: name W_V, W_O, the FFN and depth as where expressive power actually lives, say the lesson reaches them, and do not explain them now.

proof.title: Attention weights are not explanations
proof.techniqueHint: Not a proof, and labelled as one deliberately: this block records an empirical finding and a limit on what the lesson claims.
proof.goal: $\text{A large } \alpha_{ij} \text{ does not license a causal claim about the model's output.}$
proof.prompt: The remark block, and it is explicitly NOT a proof - say so if asked. It is the structural rest beat between the two halves of the scene, and it exists because 97.09% is a striking number that actively teaches a false inference if left alone. Present the finding and the rebuttal honestly: Jain & Wallace (2019) show alternative attention distributions can yield identical predictions and that adversarial patterns can be constructed; Wiegreffe & Pinter (2019) rebut in part, arguing the claim depends on what one demands of an explanation and on the baseline. Do NOT resolve the debate and do not turn this into an interpretability lecture. The lesson's own claim is narrow and should be repeated as such: the mechanism - what the weights do and what they cannot do. Note that this block is the only uncoloured one in the lesson, and that the absence of highlighting is the signal.

steps.label: The empirical finding
steps.justification: Jain & Wallace (2019), *Attention is not Explanation*: on a range of classification tasks, attention weights correlate poorly with gradient-based feature importance, and adversarial attention distributions can be constructed that differ substantially while leaving the model's predictions essentially unchanged.
steps.explanation: Wiegreffe & Pinter (2019), *Attention is not not Explanation*, rebut this in part: the adversarial distributions are found by an attack that is free to search outside what training would ever produce, and whether attention 'explains' depends on the baseline and on what one demands of an explanation. The debate is live. What is not in dispute is that a large weight, on its own, is not evidence of causal dependence.
steps.prompt: Give the finding and the rebuttal together - presenting either alone is a distortion. Do not adjudicate. If pressed for a bottom line: a large attention weight is a fact about mixing, and turning it into a causal claim about the output requires evidence this lesson has not shown.

steps.label: What this lesson claims
steps.justification: The mechanism: what the weights do, what they are constrained to do, and what they cannot do. Not: why the model produced what it produced.
steps.explanation:
Everything this scene asserts is checkable on screen — the row sums at six decimals, the divisor, the hull the output cannot leave. None of it is an interpretability claim, and the $0.970889$ on *cat* is not an exception: our $W_Q$ and $W_K$ were **built** to put it there.

This block is the only uncoloured one in the lesson. That is deliberate: every other panel is a derivation, and this one is commentary.
